lead: This unit explains how quantum circuits turn superposition and interference into algorithms. You learn the standard circuit for each algorithm, the state before measurement, and the classical post-processing. By the end you can trace Deutsch-Jozsa, QFT, phase estimation, Shor and Grover on paper, and say what BQP does and does not promise.
about: The unit starts with quantum parallelism and phase kickback (4.1), the two circuit effects reused everywhere. Chapters 4.2 and 4.3 use them for Deutsch, Deutsch-Jozsa, Bernstein-Vazirani and Simon. Chapter 4.4 builds the quantum Fourier transform; 4.5 uses it for phase estimation and order finding. Chapter 4.6 turns order finding into Shor's factoring algorithm. Chapter 4.7 moves to amplitude amplification in Grover search; 4.8 adds quantum counting and the query lower bound. Chapter 4.9 places these results in complexity classes, especially BQP, and explains why NP-complete problems still lack an exponential quantum speedup.

chapters.idea: A quantum circuit can evaluate a function on all inputs in superposition in one oracle call, but phase kickback writes the result into signs that later interference can use.
chapters.depth: Define quantum parallelism as evaluating a function on a uniform superposition: H^⊗n|0^n⟩ = (1/√(2^n))Σ_x|x⟩. Define the oracle U_f|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y⊕f(x)⟩, where x is an n-bit input, y is an ancilla bit, and ⊕ is XOR. Show that measuring the first register gives one x, not all values. Derive phase kickback: if U_f|x⟩|−⟩ = (−1)^f(x)|x⟩|−⟩, with |−⟩ = (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2. Distinguish global phase from relative phase. Some syllabi spell it phase kick-back.

figure.title: Quantum parallelism and phase kickback
figure.caption: The ancilla in |−⟩ turns each function value into a sign on the matching input state; the output remains a superposition until measured.
figure.aria: A flow diagram shows an n-qubit input going through Hadamards, then a controlled oracle with an ancilla in the minus state, producing phase kickback and a superposed output.

chapters.example: Question: take n=2, f(x)=x1⊕x2 (parity of the two bits), ancilla |−⟩, and input |00⟩. After H on both qubits the state is (1/2)(|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)|−⟩. After U_f the state is (1/2)(|00⟩−|01⟩−|10⟩+|11⟩)|−⟩. The signs are (−1)^f(x); the |−⟩ ancilla is unchanged.
chapters.trap: Thinking one oracle call lets you read f(0), f(1), ... by measurement. Measurement collapses to one x; algorithms must use interference to turn relative phases into a useful amplitude.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: Hadamard, CNOT; Unit 2: superposition and measurement.
chapters.leave: Specific algorithms to 4.2 and 4.3; QFT to 4.4.

chapters.idea: Deutsch and Deutsch-Jozsa decide a promised property of a Boolean function with one oracle query by converting phase signs into a measurable bit.
chapters.depth: Deutsch problem: decide if f:{0,1}→{0,1} is constant or balanced with one query. Circuit: |0⟩|1⟩, H on both, U_f, H on the first qubit, measure. Result: 0 means constant, 1 means balanced. Deutsch-Jozsa (DJ) extends this to n bits with the promise that f is constant or balanced, where balanced means f is 1 on exactly half of the 2^n inputs. Start |0^n⟩|1⟩, apply H^⊗n to the input register and H to the ancilla, apply U_f, apply H^⊗n again, then measure. The all-zero outcome is certain for constant f and never occurs for balanced f.

figure.title: Deutsch-Jozsa circuit
figure.caption: The final Hadamards convert the relative signs into an all-zero outcome for a constant function.
figure.aria: A left-to-right circuit diagram shows an input register passing through Hadamards, a controlled oracle with an ancilla, another Hadamard layer, and measurement.

chapters.example: Question: in a 2-qubit Deutsch-Jozsa test, f(00)=0, f(01)=1, f(10)=1, f(11)=0. What is the probability of measuring 00 after the final Hadamards? Answer: the amplitude of 00 is (1/4)Σ_x(−1)^f(x) = (1/4)(1−1−1+1)=0, so the probability is 0. The function is balanced.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the final Hadamard layer, or confusing the one-qubit Deutsch circuit with the n-qubit Deutsch-Jozsa circuit. The DJ promise is essential; without it the answer is not deterministic.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 phase kickback; Unit 3: Hadamard and controlled gates.
chapters.leave: Bernstein-Vazirani and Simon to 4.3; phase estimation to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Bernstein-Vazirani reads a hidden bit string in one query, while Simon finds a hidden period by collecting linear equations from repeated measurements.
chapters.depth: Bernstein-Vazirani (BV): promised f(x)=s·x mod 2 for an unknown n-bit string s, where s·x is the bitwise inner product modulo 2. The circuit is the DJ circuit; the final Hadamards leave exactly |s⟩ with probability 1. Classically n queries are needed. Simon problem: promised f(x)=f(y) iff y=x⊕s for an unknown nonzero s; s is the period. Use two n-qubit registers, H^⊗n on the first, U_f, H^⊗n on the first, then measure the first register. A result y satisfies y·s=0 mod 2. Repeat O(n) times and solve the linear system for s.

figure.title: Simon circuit
figure.caption: One register is measured after the second Hadamard layer; each result gives a linear equation on the hidden period.
figure.aria: A downward circuit diagram shows two input registers, a Hadamard layer on the first, a joint oracle, a second Hadamard layer, and measurement of the first register.

chapters.example: Question: Bernstein-Vazirani with n=3 and secret s=101, so f(x)=x1⊕x3 mod 2. Start with |000⟩|−⟩, apply H to the three input qubits, apply U_f, then apply H again. What is measured? Answer: |101⟩ with probability 1, because the phase is (−1)^(s·x) and the final Hadamards invert the Fourier transform.
chapters.trap: Thinking Simon outputs s directly. Simon gives random y with y·s=0; you must repeat and solve equations. Also, BV needs the promise f(x)=s·x mod 2.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 Deutsch-Jozsa circuit; Unit 3: Hadamard and oracle construction.
chapters.leave: Hidden subgroup problem and Shor to 4.6; detailed linear algebra to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: The quantum Fourier transform changes basis so that hidden periods become measurable phases.
chapters.depth: Define the QFT on N=2^n basis states: QFT|j⟩ = (1/√N)Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} e^(2πijk/N)|k⟩, where i is the imaginary unit and e is Euler's number. Give the inverse QFT. Build the circuit from Hadamards and controlled phase gates R_k, then swaps to correct qubit order. Show the product form for n qubits. Applications: phase estimation, period finding, Shor factoring. Some syllabi call it quantum Fourier transform (QFT).

figure.title: QFT circuit
figure.caption: The QFT circuit uses Hadamards, controlled phase gates and a final swap to set qubit order.
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow diagram shows an n-qubit input going through Hadamards, controlled phase gates, swaps, and producing a Fourier state.

chapters.example: Question: for N=4 (n=2), find QFT|01⟩. Answer: QFT|01⟩ = (1/2)(|00⟩ + i|01⟩ − |10⟩ − i|11⟩), because the amplitude of |k⟩ is e^(2πi·1·k/4)/2.
chapters.trap: Using Hadamards alone for n>1; the QFT needs controlled phase gates. Also check the sign of the exponent and the qubit order used by your convention.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: Hadamard and controlled phase gates; Unit 1: complex numbers and tensor products.

chapters.idea: Phase estimation reads the eigenphase of a unitary, and order finding applies it to the multiplication map modulo N.
chapters.depth: Quantum phase estimation (QPE): given U|u⟩=e^(2πiφ)|u⟩, estimate φ. Use a t-qubit first register, H^⊗t, controlled-U^(2^j) operations, then inverse QFT. Measuring gives a t-bit approximation to φ. Order finding: for N and a coprime a, the order r is the smallest positive r with a^r≡1 mod N. Use U|x⟩=|ax mod N⟩ and phase estimation; measured values approximate s/r. Continued fractions recover r. Some syllabi call it quantum phase estimation or order-finding.

figure.title: Phase estimation and order finding
figure.caption: The first register is measured after the inverse QFT; the second register stays in the eigenstate |u⟩.
figure.aria: A downward circuit diagram shows a phase register passing through Hadamards, a controlled unitary with an eigenvector register, an inverse QFT, and measurement.

chapters.example: Question: for N=15 and a=2, order r=4. What phase φ does phase estimation aim to read, and what 3-bit value is closest? Answer: φ=s/r for s=0,1,2,3; for s=1, φ=1/4=0.25. With t=3, 0.25×8=2, so the register reads 010. Continued fraction 2/8=1/4 gives r=4.
chapters.trap: Forgetting continued fractions: the measured value y/2^t is an approximation to s/r, not r itself. Also, a non-coprime a already gives a factor.
chapters.leave: Shor's factoring steps to 4.6; complexity to 4.9.

chapters.idea: Shor factors N by finding the order r of a random base a modulo N and using gcd to turn that order into factors.
chapters.depth: Reduce factoring to order finding. Choose a with 1<a<N and gcd(a,N)=1; if gcd(a,N)>1 you already have a factor. Use phase estimation to find the order r of a mod N. If r is even and a^(r/2)≠−1 mod N, compute gcd(a^(r/2)−1,N) and gcd(a^(r/2)+1,N). One of these is a nontrivial factor. Repeat with a new a on failure. Some syllabi call it Shor's factorization algorithm.

figure.title: Shor's factoring loop
figure.caption: A failed parity or trivial-root check returns the algorithm to a new base a.
figure.aria: A downward flowchart shows choosing a base, order finding, checking whether r is even and the half-power is nontrivial, then computing gcd factors, with a dashed retry loop.

chapters.example: Question: factor N=15 using a=2. The order is r=4 because 2^4=16≡1 mod 15. Then a^(r/2)=2^2=4. Compute gcd(4−1,15)=gcd(3,15)=3 and gcd(4+1,15)=gcd(5,15)=5. The factors are 3 and 5.
chapters.trap: Using a^r±1 instead of a^(r/2)±1, or forgetting to check that r is even and a^(r/2)≠−1 mod N.
chapters.leave: BQP and NP-complete comparison to 4.9; QFT details to 4.4.

chapters.idea: Grover search amplifies the amplitude of a marked item in an unstructured list using about √N oracle calls.
chapters.depth: Problem: one marked item among N=2^n items. The oracle flips the sign of the marked item. The diffusion operator inverts amplitudes about their mean. The Grover iteration is oracle plus diffusion. The state stays in a two-dimensional plane; the angle satisfies sin θ=1/√N. After k iterations the success probability is sin²((2k+1)θ). Optimal k is about (π/4)√N. Circuit: H^⊗n, repeat oracle and diffusion, measure. Some syllabi call it Grover's quantum search algorithm.

figure.caption: The success probability peaks near three iterations for 16 items, then falls; extra iterations spoil the search.
figure.aria: A line plot of success probability against Grover iterations for 16 items rises to a peak near three iterations and then falls.

chapters.example: Question: N=16, one marked item. Grover uses θ=arcsin(1/√16)=0.2527 rad. After k iterations, success probability is sin²((2k+1)θ). Find the best k among 0,1,2,3 and the probability at k=3. Answer: probabilities are 0.0625, 0.472, 0.908, 0.961; best k=3, P≈0.961.
chapters.trap: Running more than the optimal number of iterations; the probability falls after the peak. Also, the oracle must be a quantum query, not a classical check of each item.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 phase kickback; Unit 3: Hadamard and oracle construction.
chapters.leave: Quantum counting and lower bound to 4.8; NP-complete complexity to 4.9.

chapters.idea: Quantum counting estimates how many marked items exist by applying phase estimation to the Grover operator, and the √N query lower bound shows Grover is optimal up to constants.
chapters.depth: Quantum counting combines Grover with phase estimation. Let M be the number of marked items and θ=arcsin(√(M/N)). The Grover operator has eigenvalues e^(±2iθ). Phase estimation on a t-qubit register estimates θ/π to t bits; then M≈N sin²θ. This counts marked items without finding them. Optimality: any quantum search of an unstructured list needs Ω(√N) oracle queries; Grover uses O(√N), so the speedup is quadratic and optimal in query complexity. Only a few universities prove the lower bound in full; others state it and use the adversary idea. Some syllabi call it quantum counting and search lower bounds.

figure.title: Quantum counting
figure.caption: Phase estimation on the Grover operator gives the angle θ, and M follows from sin²θ = M/N.
figure.aria: A downward flow diagram shows phase and search registers going through Hadamards, a controlled Grover operator, an inverse QFT, estimation of θ, and computation of M.

chapters.example: Question: N=100, M=9 marked. Find θ and the 8-bit phase-estimation output y closest to 256θ/π. Answer: θ=arcsin(√(9/100))=arcsin(0.3)=0.3047 rad; θ/π=0.09699; 256×0.09699=24.83, so y=25. Reconstructing gives M≈100 sin²(π×25/256)≈9.1, rounded to 9.
chapters.trap: Thinking counting identifies which items are marked; it only estimates how many. The lower bound is on oracle queries, not on total gate count.
chapters.leave: Amplitude amplification variants and quantum walk to advanced courses; complexity classes to 4.9.

chapters.idea: BQP is the class of decision problems a quantum computer can solve in polynomial time with bounded error; it contains factoring, but it is not known to contain NP-complete problems.
chapters.depth: Define P, NP, and BQP, where BQP means bounded-error quantum polynomial time: a polynomial-size quantum circuit decides the answer with error at most 1/3. Known relations include P⊆BQP and BQP⊆PSPACE. Whether BQP contains NP, or equals NP, is open. Shor puts integer factoring in BQP. NP-complete problems have no known polynomial quantum algorithm; Grover gives only a quadratic speedup over brute force. Some syllabi call BQP bounded quantum polynomial time.

figure.caption: Solid arrows are known inclusions; the dashed link between BQP and NP is not settled.
figure.aria: A graph of complexity classes shows P inside BQP and NP, BQP and NP inside PSPACE, NP-complete inside NP, factoring placed in BQP, and a dashed unknown relation between BQP and NP.

chapters.example: Question: a Boolean satisfiability instance has n=50 variables. Compare classical brute force with Grover. Answer: classical search checks up to 2^50≈1.13×10^15 assignments; Grover needs about (π/4)√(2^50)≈2.6×10^7 oracle calls. This is a quadratic speedup, still exponential in n; no polynomial quantum algorithm is known for NP-complete problems.
chapters.trap: Thinking Shor solves NP-complete problems because factoring is hard classically. Factoring is in BQP, but it is not known to be NP-complete. Grover gives only a quadratic speedup.
chapters.prereq: 4.6 Shor; 4.7 Grover; Unit 1: basic complexity notation.
chapters.leave: Detailed complexity proofs and polynomial method to advanced courses; quantum walk and amplitude amplification to advanced study.
